summary:
Last Message Home

Chat with your robots! Last Message Home is an interactive web application that tells you the tales of lost NASA spacecrafts and robots. You can chat with 10 robots, including Viking 1, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity, and Pioneer 10, sent on missions across Mars, the Moon, and deep space.

By chatting to the robots you will find out what they discovered, what they achieved, and what we know about their last message and what happened at the end of their missions! Every reply has a category to help you understand what it is telling you. Either FACT (information from NASA), SUM (calculated time lines), NOTE (unknown information) or STORY (creative writing). All facts have a source from NASA.

There are discovery cards using pictures from NASA, interactive quizzes, stickers to collect and an exploration map! This project helps overcome the issue of keeping the legacy of these forgotten space equipment by turning this into an easy to understand STORY. This reminds us that even though these robots have gone quiet, we should never forget what they have discovered and how they have helped us explore space!
details:
Last Message Home is an interactive, phone-style messaging web application that transforms the history of abandoned NASA spacecraft and robotic explorers into an engaging storytelling experience. It features 10 robotic missions and pieces of hardware associated with Mars, the Moon, and deep space, including Viking 1, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity, Surveyor 3, Apollo 12 ALSEP, and Pioneer 10.

Instead of presenting users with lengthy scientific documents, the application allows them to interact with these robotic explorers through predefined questions and first-person responses. Each robot shares information about its mission, achievements, discoveries, and final communications. Every response is classified using four categories: FACT, SUM, NOTE, and STORY. FACT represents information directly supported by NASA sources, SUM represents calculations derived from documented dates, NOTE identifies information that NASA does not specify, and STORY contains creative fictional narration that adds emotional depth without introducing unsupported scientific claims.

Users can explore NASA discovery cards, view original supporting quotations, access official source links, participate in interactive quizzes, collect digital stickers, and explore a map displaying the locations of robotic equipment for which NASA provides coordinates.

The primary objective is to make space exploration history accessible and interesting, particularly for students and younger audiences. By transforming historical mission archives into interactive conversations, the project encourages curiosity about space science, planetary exploration, robotics, and engineering. It also promotes scientific literacy by clearly distinguishing verified information from calculations, unknown details, and creative storytelling.

The application was developed using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript for its interface and functionality, with JSON for structured mission data and conversation content. Python 3 was used for retrieving NASA source material, while Node.js was used for automated testing and verification. Browser LocalStorage maintains collected stickers. Git and GitHub support source-code management, and GitHub Pages provides public web hosting. AI-assisted development tools, including Codex, supported implementation and debugging.

The creative aspect of the project lies in presenting abandoned spacecraft as conversational characters rather than treating them as forgotten technological objects. This approach creates an emotional connection between users and the machines that once explored distant worlds. At the same time, scientific accuracy remains a priority. Every factual response is connected to an official NASA source, and automated verification tests check quotations, numerical claims, dates, and source references. The application does not depend on live AI, external API calls, user authentication, or a backend service during normal operation, making it lightweight, accessible, and easy to use through a public web link.

During development, our team considered scientific reliability, accessibility, performance, educational value, transparency, and maintainability. We designed the experience to work across mobile phones, tablets, and desktop browsers without requiring installation or registration. The structured data architecture and automated verification system also make it easier to maintain the content and introduce additional missions in the future.

Ultimately, Last Message Home aims to preserve the legacy of humanity's robotic explorers through technology, education, and storytelling. These machines may have stopped communicating, but their discoveries, contributions, and stories deserve to remain part of humanity's journey into space.
